issues.current: IDPH will issue a regular license within 120 days after receipt of an application that qualifies; first-time licensees receive a probationary license
issues.correct: A first-time licensee gets a probationary license first. 77 IAC 295.800 says IDPH may issue it within 90 days after a completed application, and it is valid for 120 days. IDPH then reviews the establishment within the 30 days before it expires and issues the regular license if the establishment qualifies. A second probationary license of up to 120 days is possible. Applicant-to-regular-license time can therefore run well past 120 days.
issues.evidence: 77 IAC 295.800: "The Department may issue a probationary license within 90 days after receipt of a completed application"; 210 ILCS 9/40: "valid for 120 days", renewable once for up to 120 days.
issues.fix: Replace the '120 days to regular license' claim with the probationary-license sequence (probationary license within about 90 days of a complete application, valid 120 days, regular-license review in the last 30 days, one possible 120-day extension). Size lease contingencies and the ramp-up deficit to roughly 7–11 months. I could not open 295.600 (the ilga.gov page was blocked), so any '120 days' wording there is unverified.

issues.current: A 2012 proposed text mentions 20 hours every two years for directors. This is not verified against the current code.
issues.correct: The 20-hour requirement is current statute. It is a condition of licensure under 210 ILCS 9/35. Section 35 also ties director qualifications to completing an approved program within 6 months after hiring.
issues.evidence: 210 ILCS 9/35: "the director of an establishment must participate in at least 20 hours of training every 2 years"
issues.fix: State that 210 ILCS 9/35 requires director training of at least 20 hours every 2 years as a licensure condition. Add a training-hours line to the calendar and budget. Note that the statute and the rule call the position 'director', not 'manager'.

issues.current: Benefits modeled as a flat 5% operator estimate. No line for statutory paid leave.
issues.correct: Employers outside Chicago and Cook County generally owe paid leave under the Illinois Paid Leave for All Workers Act (820 ILCS 192; 40 hours per year). Chicago and Cook County each have their own paid-leave ordinances, which are more generous than the state's (Chicago's is the Paid Leave and Paid Sick and Safe Leave Ordinance). Chicago's Fair Workweek Ordinance covers healthcare employers that meet its employee-count threshold.
issues.evidence: Search results confirm Chicago and Cook County separate wage ordinances and the Fair Workweek compensation threshold ($33.85/hr). I did not fetch the paid-leave statutes, so the leave details come from general knowledge and are unverified here.
issues.fix: Add an explicit paid-leave accrual cost (about 2–4% of direct-care payroll, more for 24/7 coverage that needs replacement staff). Cite the applicable state, Chicago or Cook County ordinance. Verify each rule on the Illinois Department of Labor and municipal sites.
